Quick Dollar Drawdown Estimator (2000–2025 Historical Data)

Many retirees assume owning QQQ protects them from single-stock risk because it holds 100 companies. Look closer at crisis correlation, however, and QQQ behaves like a single duration-sensitive technology bet whenever real yields jump or capital expenditure slows.

After peaking in March 2000, Nasdaq-100 holders endured an 82.9% decline and waited roughly 14 years on a price basis to revisit that high watermark. In 2022 alone, QQQ slipped 35.1% while US healthcare (XLV) finished near flat by year-end.

Our historical workbook does not argue against owning innovation; it measures what happens when a household pairs semiconductor growth (SMH) directly against a counter-cyclical earnings engine (XLV) and short-term T-bills (SGOV) rather than stacking overlapping tech funds.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why pair SMH with XLV instead of holding both QQQ and SMH?

QQQ and SMH share heavy semiconductor and mega-cap tech overlap, so both fall together during rate shocks. XLV holds pharmaceuticals, managed care, and medical devices with much lower crisis correlation.

What happened to QQQ vs SMH x XLV during the 2022 interest-rate hike cycle?

In 2022, QQQ fell 35.1% and SMH fell 43.1%, whereas XLV held near -12.9% max drawdown, cushioning the combined two-pillar study to roughly -14.6%.
